title: Gideon and the House
premise: Zephyrine Lockridge, a pest controller who treats the supernatural as a pest-control problem, is hired by the dying village of Hollowmere to deal with 'something with fingerprints' appearing on windows, walls, and finally skin. When the church bell that was melted down in 1911 rings across the frost, Zeph discovers the house at the village's heart — Gideon House — keeps its residents alive through a covenant sealed in 1974, when the villagers stole a child from a traveling family and gave her to the house. To survive the winter and free Hollowmere, Zeph must return what was taken: not the child, long dead, but her name, which the house has been wearing like a coat. In the end he gives the house his own name in exchange for the village's release, becoming the new thing with fingerprints — loyal to people who will never know the truth of him.
about_author: Q. M. Delacroix is the pen name of a former building surveyor who spent a decade inspecting derelict English country houses and swears one of them inspected back. They write horror rooted in rural decay, bureaucratic dread, and the quiet violence of small communities keeping secrets.

chapters.title: The Callout
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. A routine vermin call in Hollowmere turns strange when Zeph finds handprints pressed into the inside of sealed windows — prints too large, too many joints. He logs it as vandalism, pockets his fee, and drives off. Emotional beat: professional contempt masking a flicker of unease he refuses to name.

chapters.title: Bellweather
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. At a motorway services, every radio in the car park plays the same tolling bell. The attendant mentions Hollowmere's bell was melted in 1911 and recast into munitions. Zeph's phone shows eleven missed calls from the village, all timestamped before he left. Emotional beat: the rational world developing hairline cracks.

chapters.title: Terms of Engagement
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. He returns under contract: the parish council offers triple rate to stay until the frost breaks. He meets Edith Marlowe, 94, who watches him with pity rather than hope. She says the house doesn't want pests removed; it wants a witness. Emotional beat: Zeph taking a job he tells himself is just money.

chapters.title: Gideon House
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. First survey of the house: warm rooms in an unheated ruin, dust arranged in neat rows, a nursery that appears on no floor plan. He finds a child's ledger where every villager's name is written and struck through except one blank line dated 1974. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into violation.

chapters.title: The Villagers' Version
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. At the Fox and Hare, the villagers are uniformly friendly, uniformly rehearsed. Their stories about 1974 differ by one detail each — the season, the family's surname, the color of the van. Zeph realizes they're not lying; they're reciting something they were made to remember wrong. Emotional beat: loneliness among warmth.

chapters.title: Frostwork
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. Overnight frost patterns the windows in shapes: a door, a small hand, letters. The pattern spells a fragment — 'EL—'. Edith nearly faints seeing it and begs him to leave before the first hard frost completes. Emotional beat: protective instinct arriving ahead of belief.

chapters.title: What Edith Kept
chapters.summary: POV Edith Marlowe. Flashback chapter: 1974, young Edith watching the village vote — a show of hands in the church — to give the traveling family's daughter, Elenora, to Gideon House so the mine would reopen and winter would spare them. Emotional beat: guilt preserved like a specimen.

chapters.title: Something with Fingerprints
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. The prints appear on Zeph's own skin after he sleeps in the house — rising up his arms like a tide line. Each morning they're higher. He photographs them; the photos show only unmarked skin. Emotional beat: the skeptic's body outvoting the skeptic's mind.

chapters.title: The Bell Rings Again
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. The melted bell tolls at dawn and every villager stops mid-motion, faces slack, then resumes as if nothing happened — except their shadows now face the house regardless of sun. Zeph follows his own shadow, which has begun leaning toward Gideon House too. Emotional beat: horror of complicity.

chapters.title: Records and Ruin
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. In the county archive he finds the 1911 melting order and a 1974 missing-persons file: Elenora Voss, age nine, last seen at Gideon House. The investigating officer's notes end mid-sentence, the handwriting shifting to match the ledger's. Emotional beat: truth assembling itself against resistance.

chapters.title: Edith Breaks
chapters.summary: POV Edith. Present day: Edith confesses to Zeph that she seconded the motion in 1974, that the house granted them forty years of mild winters and full larders, and that the debt comes due when the last witness dies — which is her, this winter. Emotional beat: confession as both relief and detonation.

chapters.title: The Village Turns
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. After Edith's confession spreads, the villagers stop pretending: they need a replacement witness, and Zeph — outsider, contracted, marked — is the obvious candidate. His truck's tires are slashed; the road out frosts over in July-thick rime. Emotional beat: betrayal wearing welcoming faces.

chapters.title: Negotiating with the Nursery
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. Zeph confronts the house directly, speaking aloud in the impossible nursery. It answers through the frost: it will release the village if someone freely takes Elenora's place — but it wants more than a body. It wants a name given willingly, worn willingly. Emotional beat: bargaining with something patient.

chapters.title: Elenora
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. Researching the Voss family, Zeph learns Elenora's mother died never knowing, and that 'Elenora' means the house can wear her forever — a stolen identity as much as a stolen child. The prints on his arms reach his collarbone. Emotional beat: grief for a stranger fifty years gone.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. Zeph attempts restitution: he speaks Elenora's true name back to the house, formally returning it. The house convulses — walls breathing, frost screaming — but refuses. A name returned must be replaced, not merely surrendered. The first hard frost begins forming on the fields. Emotional beat: hope raised and dashed in one night.

chapters.title: The Last Witness
chapters.summary: POV Edith. Dying, Edith gives Zeph her testimony to carry out — but the road stays frozen, phones dead, the village sealed like a snow globe. She asks him not to save her but to remember correctly, since remembering wrongly is how the house kept them all. Emotional beat: love expressed as accuracy.

chapters.title: Loyalty vs. Truth
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. The villagers, desperate, try to force Zeph into the nursery themselves — loyalty to their own survival overriding everything. He escapes into the house's interior, realizing the house protects him from them: it wants a willing gift, not a sacrificed one. Emotional beat: understanding the difference between being taken and giving.

chapters.title: The Final Pattern
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. The frost writes its near-final pattern: Elenora's full name, almost complete, one letter short. Zeph understands the house isn't demanding a replacement victim — it's dying of anonymity, unable to be remembered without a name to hold. Emotional beat: terror transmuting into terrible compassion.

chapters.title: The Gift
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. Climax. In the nursery, before the assembled villagers and the ringing of the unmelted bell, Zeph willingly gives the house his name — Zephyrine Lockridge — spoken freely, witnessed truly. The frost completes Elenora's name and releases her; the prints on his skin sink beneath the surface like stones in water. Emotional beat: sacrifice chosen, not extracted.

chapters.title: Thaw
chapters.summary: POV Zephyrine. The frost breaks; roads open; the bell falls silent mid-toll. But Zeph cannot leave — the house holds his name, and without it he frays at the edges when he crosses the gate. He remains as caretaker, sending postcards signed only 'Z.' Emotional beat: bittersweet captivity.

chapters.title: What the Village Remembers
chapters.summary: POV Edith's granddaughter, Ruth. Months later, Ruth visits the house to thank its strange caretaker and finds the ledger updated: every villager's name restored, Elenora Voss written whole, and a new entry — 'witness: willing.' The village remembers 1974 correctly now, all of them, all at once. Emotional beat: truth as the only lasting monument.

chapters.title: Something with Fingerprints (Reprise)
chapters.summary: POV Ruth. Leaving Hollowmere, Ruth finds small handprints on her car window — too many joints, pressed from the outside — and beneath them, traced in frost, a single letter: Z. She smiles, wipes it away, and drives toward the thaw. Emotional beat: haunting transformed into guardianship; the price of survival paid forward.
